what: The Electricity Bill Calculator turns the units (kWh) on your meter into an estimated bill. You can use one flat price per unit, as most suppliers in Europe, North America and Australia do, or a slab (tiered) table where the price per unit rises as you use more, as in much of Asia and Africa.

Start from "My own rates" or a preset for the United States, United Kingdom, Delhi in India, Bangladesh or Pakistan. Every rate is editable, because electricity prices change often. Add fixed charges, a per-unit adjustment and taxes, and the breakdown shows exactly where the money goes.
Everything is worked out in your browser as you type.
uses: See whether the amount on your bill matches the units and rates.
Read your meter mid-month and estimate the bill so there are no surprises.
See the cost of crossing a slab
Find out how much more a few extra units cost when they push you into a higher slab.
Try a flat rate against a slab table to see which is cheaper for your usage.
Work out each flat's bill from its sub-meter readings.
tutorial: In "Start from" keep "My own rates (any country)" or pick a preset. A preset fills in the rates, taxes and currency and shows the date they were published.
Pick "One flat rate per unit" if every unit costs the same, or "Slab rates" if the price changes with usage.
Type the units (kWh) from your bill in "Units used", or open "Work out units from meter readings" and type the previous and current readings.
In slab mode, change "Up to unit" and "Rate per unit" for each slab. Leave the last "Up to unit" empty to mean "and above". Use "Add slab" or ✕ to change the number of slabs.
"Each slab at its own rate" is the most common. "One previous slab benefit" and "All units at the final slab's rate" match some utilities; an example under the list explains each.
Fill in any per-unit adjustment, fixed charges, sales tax or VAT, a second tax or duty, and charges with no tax (such as a TV fee).
The estimated bill, average price per unit and a line-by-line breakdown appear instantly. Use "Copy breakdown" to save it.
features: Works for almost any country's residential tariff.
US, UK, Delhi, Bangladesh and three Pakistan tables, each with the date and a reminder to check current rates.
Progressive slabs, one-previous-slab benefit, and whole-bill-at-final-slab.
Subtract two readings to get your units.
Two percentage taxes on energy and fixed charges, plus untaxed charges.
Guesses your currency from your browser and lets you type any symbol.
Each slab, charge and tax on its own line, ready to copy.

example.title: Worked example: 250 units with slabs
example.text: Slabs are 1–100 at 10, 101–200 at 15 and 201+ at 20 per unit, applied "each slab at its own rate". For 250 units: 100 × 10 = 1,000, plus 100 × 15 = 1,500, plus 50 × 20 = 1,000, so energy is 3,500. Add a fixed charge of 100 and 5% VAT on both: (3,500 + 100) × 1.05 = 3,780. The breakdown lists each of these lines.

tips: Copy the exact rates from your latest bill; they change more often than you think.
Fuel price or cost adjustments usually go in "Extra per unit" and can be negative.
If your bill has a daily standing charge, multiply it by the days in the bill and put it in fixed charges.
Try 5 or 10 units less to see whether staying under a slab limit would save money.
The average price per unit is handy for the Appliance Energy Cost Calculator.
problems: The total is lower than my real bill
Your bill may include meter rent, arrears, late fees, other taxes or a fuel adjustment. Add them in the charges fields.
It says a slab must end at a higher unit
Each "Up to unit" must be bigger than the one above it. Check for a typo in the table.
My units go past the last slab
Leave the last "Up to unit" empty so it means "and above", or add another slab.
That is expected: prices change. Edit the numbers in the table to match your bill.
